substitute for professional legal advice. For details of government approvals obtained by us, see the section titled “Government
and Other Approvals” on page no. 239 of this Red Herring Prospectus

GENERAL CORPORATE LAWS

The Companies Act, 2013:

The Companies Act, 2013 provides a comprehensive legal framework for the formation, governance, management, and
regulation of jewellery businesses incorporated as companies in India, covering incorporation procedures, shareholding
structures, corporate governance norms, and the roles and duties of directors and Key Managerial Personnel (KMPs) to ensure
transparency and accountability. It is particularly relevant to jewellers in areas such as capital raising through shares or
debentures, mergers and acquisitions, restructuring, and corporate financing, while also mandating the maintenance of statutory
registers, audits, and annual financial reporting. The Act further safeguards minority shareholders’ rights and provides
mechanisms for dispute resolution, which are especially important in family-run or closely held jewellery firms. Additionally,
under Section 135 on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), eligible companies must contribute to social initiatives,
promoting ethical practices. Overall, compliance with the Act helps jewellery companies operate legally, build stakeholder
confidence, and achieve sustainable growth in a competitive, high-value industry.

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016:

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 provides a structured and time-bound legal framework for resolving
insolvency and financial distress in jewellery businesses, whether operating as sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLPs, or
companies. It enables a jeweller in default of payments to creditors, suppliers, or financial institutions to undergo the Corporate
Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), which may be initiated by the business itself or by any financial or operational creditor,
whether secured or unsecured. The Code aims to preserve the economic value of the business by facilitating its restructuring,
sale, or revival within a prescribed period, subject to extension in specific cases. It also protects the interests of key stakeholders,
including employees, suppliers of gold, diamonds, and other materials, banks, and customers who have made advance
payments. Overall, the IBC offers a transparent, enforceable, and collective mechanism for addressing financial distress,
minimizing prolonged disputes, and supporting business continuity, thereby strengthening stakeholder confidence in the
jewellery sector.

SEBI Act, Rules and Regulations:

The SEBI Act, 1992, along with its rules and regulations, applies to jewellery companies that are listed or intend to raise capital
through the securities market, imposing strict compliance requirements to ensure transparency, accountability, and investor
protection. Jewellers must adhere to provisions relating to the issue and allotment of securities, listing and delisting, continuous
disclosure obligations, insider trading restrictions, and substantial acquisition of shares. Key regulations include the SEBI
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 for periodic disclosures and financial transparency; the
SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 governing public and rights issues; the SEBI
(Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 to prevent misuse of unpublished price-sensitive information; and the SEBI
(Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 regulating major share acquisitions and takeovers.
Compliance with these frameworks enables jewellery companies to maintain investor confidence, uphold market integrity,
avoid regulatory penalties, and efficiently raise capital for expansion, acquisitions, and modernization of operations.




                                                                                                                              162
Transfer of Property Act, 1882:

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 governs the legal transfer of immovable property and related interests, making it highly
relevant for jewellers in relation to boutiques, manufacturing units, warehouses, and other business premises. It permits
transactions such as sale, mortgage, lease, exchange, and creation of charges, each carrying specific legal implications—for
instance, purchasing property through a sale deed, securing loans via mortgages on business premises, or operating outlets
under lease agreements. Temporary use arrangements, such as exhibition spaces, may fall under leave and license without
transferring ownership interests. The Act ensures that only lawful rights and interests held by the transferor can be transferred,
thereby protecting jewellers from disputes over title or encumbrances. Compliance with requirements relating to registration,
stamping, and documentation ensures that property rights are legally valid, enforceable, and recognized by courts, facilitating
smooth operations, access to financing, and expansion of jewellery businesses.

The Registration Act, 1908:

The Registration Act, 1908 establishes the legal framework for the registration of documents relating to immovable property
and certain transactions, which is particularly relevant for jewellers in respect of their boutiques, shops, manufacturing units,
and warehouses. It mandates the compulsory registration of non-testamentary instruments that create, assign, limit, or
extinguish rights in immovable property—such as sale deeds, long-term lease agreements, and mortgages—commonly used by
jewellers when acquiring or leasing commercial premises. The Act also permits optional registration of other documents,
enhancing their evidentiary value in case of disputes. For jewellers, proper registration ensures legal recognition and
enforceability of property and tenancy rights, strengthens agreements with landlords and financial institutions, and reduces the
risk of future litigation over ownership or encumbrances. Overall, compliance with the Act supports secure property
transactions and facilitates the smooth operation and expansion of jewellery businesses.

The Specific Relief Act, 1963:

The Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a legal framework for enforcing civil rights through remedies such as specific
performance and injunctions, which is particularly significant for jewellers given the high value and unique nature of their
goods. It enables jewellers to seek enforcement of contracts involving the sale or supply of specific jewellery items, custom-
made designs, or bulk transactions in precious metals and gemstones, where monetary compensation may be inadequate due to
the uniqueness of the subject matter. Courts may direct parties to fulfill their contractual obligations—such as delivering
bespoke jewellery or honoring supply agreements—rather than merely awarding damages. The Act also allows for injunctions
to prevent breaches, such as restraining a supplier from selling reserved or exclusive items to others. By focusing on the
enforcement of contractual obligations and protection of individual rights, the Act helps jewellers safeguard their commercial
interests, ensure reliability in transactions, and maintain trust in both business-to-business and retail operations.

Sales of Goods Act, 1930:

The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 provides the legal framework governing the sale and purchase of goods, including gold, silver,
gemstones, and finished jewellery, thereby regulating transactions between jewellers, suppliers, and customers. It defines a
contract of sale as an agreement where the seller transfers or agrees to transfer ownership of goods to the buyer for a price,
covering both immediate sales and future delivery arrangements. The Act broadly defines “goods” to include all movable
property, encompassing raw materials as well as finished jewellery items. Key provisions relevant to jewellers include rules on
transfer of ownership, passing of risk, delivery obligations, and implied conditions and warranties relating to title, quality, and
conformity with description. For instance, jewellers are required to ensure that jewellery sold is free from encumbrances, meets
agreed specifications, and adheres to applicable standards such as hallmarking. The Act also provides remedies for breach of
contract, including the buyer’s right to reject defective goods or claim damages and the seller’s right to recover payment.
Overall, it promotes fair, secure, and transparent transactions in both retail and wholesale jewellery operations.

The Indian Contract Act, 1872:

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, as applied to jewellers, provides the foundational legal framework governing all contracts and
commercial transactions within the jewellery industry, including purchase and sale agreements, supply contracts, consignment
arrangements, and employment contracts. The Act ensures that contracts entered into by jewellers with suppliers, customers,
and business partners are legally enforceable, covering both general principles of contract law (Sections 1–75) such as offer,
acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, and legality of object, as well as special contracts (Sections 124–238) like

                                                                                                                         163
contracts of bailment, pledge, agency, and guarantee, which are particularly relevant in jewellery dealings. For instance,
jewellers often rely on bailment and pledge contracts when providing gold or gemstones for manufacturing or securing loans
against jewellery. Agency provisions are used when jewellers appoint sales agents or distributors, and guarantees are common
in transactions involving bank finance or credit from suppliers. By providing a structured legal framework, the Act ensures that
jewellers can securely conduct business, enforce rights, mitigate risks of breach, and resolve disputes, thereby maintaining trust
and stability in both retail and wholesale jewellery operations.

The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881:

The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 establishes the legal framework for the use, transfer, and enforcement of instruments
such as cheques, promissory notes, and bills of exchange, which are widely used by jewellers in high-value transactions and
credit arrangements. Jewellers rely on these instruments for purchasing raw materials, making payments to suppliers, and
extending credit to customers, making the Act essential for ensuring secure and legally enforceable financial dealings. It
provides remedies in cases of dishonour, particularly under Section 138, where a bounced cheque issued in transactions
involving gold, gemstones, or jewellery can result in criminal liability and facilitate recovery. The Act also regulates
endorsement, delivery, and negotiation, enabling efficient settlement of trade obligations. Further, amendments such as the
Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2018, introducing provisions like Sections 143A and 148, strengthen creditor
protection by allowing interim compensation during pending proceedings. Overall, compliance with the Act helps jewellers
safeguard financial interests, manage credit effectively, and maintain trust and stability in both retail and wholesale operations.

Information Technology Act, 2000:

The Information Technology Act, 2000 provides the legal framework for conducting secure and legally recognized electronic
transactions and maintaining digital records, which is increasingly important for jewellers adopting e-commerce, online sales,
and digital payment systems. It grants legal validity to electronic contracts, communications, and records, enabling jewellers
to replace traditional paper-based processes with efficient digital methods. The Act also facilitates the use of digital signatures
and electronic authentication to ensure the integrity and authenticity of agreements with suppliers, customers, and financial
institutions. Additionally, it addresses cybersecurity and data protection concerns, which are critical for safeguarding sensitive
customer information, payment data, and proprietary designs. Amendments, including updates to the First Schedule, have
further expanded the scope for electronic execution of documents such as agreements and invoices. Overall, compliance with
the IT Act helps jewellers reduce risks related to cyber threats, enhance operational efficiency through digitalization, and
support secure and modern business practices in the jewellery industry.

Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951:

The Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 provides a framework for licensing and regulating industrial
enterprises, but most jewellery businesses are largely exempt from licensing under the liberalized regime introduced by the
New Industrial Policy of July 24, 1991. While the Act initially required licenses for manufacturing units, jewellers producing
gold, silver, and precious or semi-precious jewellery generally do not fall under restricted or sensitive industries such as defense,
alcohol, explosives, or hazardous chemicals, allowing them to commence operations freely. However, jewellers must file an
Industrial Entrepreneurs Memorandum (IEM) with the Secretariat for Industrial Assistance (SIA) under the Department of
Industrial Policy and Promotion as a formal notification of establishing or expanding a manufacturing unit. Once the IEM is
submitted, operations may proceed without further licensing, though jewellers remain subject to other statutory obligations,
including the Jewellery (Control and Regulation) Acts, tax laws, hallmarking standards, and safety regulations. This framework
balances regulatory oversight with a liberalized business environment, fostering entrepreneurship and structured growth within
the jewellery sector.

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899:

The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 regulates the payment of stamp duty on instruments and documents executed in the course of
business, which is particularly relevant for jewellers dealing with high-value transactions. This includes sale deeds, lease
agreements, mortgages, partnership deeds, contracts for goods, and bills of exchange. Stamp duty becomes critical when
jewellers transfer ownership of commercial premises, secure loans against property or inventory, enter supplier contracts, or
execute agreements for bulk purchases of gold, gemstones, or other materials. Proper stamping ensures that such documents
are legally admissible in court, safeguarding enforceability and authenticity, while non-compliance can lead to penalties, fines,
or inadmissibility in legal proceedings. Adhering to the Stamp Act thus protects jewellers’ commercial agreements, property
rights, and financial transactions, providing legal certainty and supporting smooth operations in both retail and wholesale
jewellery businesses.
                                                                                                                           164
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides a legal framework for resolving commercial disputes outside of traditional
courts through arbitration and conciliation, which is particularly valuable for jewellers due to the high-value, specialized, and
time-sensitive nature of their transactions. Jewellery businesses can incorporate arbitration clauses in contracts with suppliers,
customers, manufacturers, or franchisees to address issues such as delayed deliveries, defective goods, payment defaults, or
breaches of agreement efficiently, confidentially, and cost-effectively. The Act regulates the appointment of arbitrators, conduct
of proceedings, enforcement of arbitral awards, and conciliation processes, allowing jewellers to maintain business continuity
without prolonged litigation. Conciliation also offers a flexible, mutually agreed approach to resolve disputes amicably,
preserving long-term business relationships in the close-knit jewellery trade. Compliance with the Act helps jewellers mitigate
financial and reputational risks, enforce contracts effectively, and secure timely resolution of both domestic and international
trade disputes.

BUSINESS AND / OR KEY INDUSTRY AND/OR TRADE RELATED LAWS AND REGULATIONS

The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016:

The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 (BIS Act), effective from October 12, 2017, provides a legal framework for
standardization, certification, and quality enforcement in India, with direct relevance to jewellery businesses. The Act mandates
hallmarking of precious metal articles, such as gold and silver, to ensure purity and build consumer trust, while requiring
manufacturers and retailers to obtain BIS certification and registration before affixing the BIS Standard Mark on products.
Non-compliance attracts penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for selling substandard items or misusing the Standard
Mark. The Act also strengthens consumer protection by empowering BIS to recall defective products and require compensation.
By enforcing adherence to prescribed quality standards, the BIS Act promotes ethical practices, safeguards consumer interests,
and enhances credibility and confidence in the jewellery industry.

The Bureau of Indian Standards (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018:

The Bureau of Indian Standards (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018, along with its 2022 amendments, establish a comprehensive
framework for jewellers to ensure authenticity, purity, and consumer protection in the sale of precious metal articles. Under
these regulations, all jewellers must obtain a BIS registration certificate for each sales premise, display it onsite, and ensure the
details are available on the BIS website. The regulations mandate hallmarking of gold and silver jewellery and artefacts, with
jewellers solely responsible for the purity and fineness of hallmarked items and liable for any discrepancies. Hallmarking is
conducted through BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, with revised fees for gold and silver payable by
jewellers and collected by BIS. From April 1, 2023, all gold items must carry a 6-digit alphanumeric Hallmark Unique
Identification (HUID), allowing consumers to trace the jeweller, verify purity, and identify the hallmarking centre. These
provisions promote compliance with quality standards, enhance consumer confidence, and ensure accountability and
transparency within the jewellery industry.

The Hallmarking of Gold Jewellery and Gold Artefacts Order, 2020:

The Hallmarking of Gold Jewellery and Gold Artefacts Orders (2020, 2021, and 2023) provide a comprehensive regulatory
framework for mandatory hallmarking and consumer protection in the jewellery sector. Under the 2020 Order, effective June
16, 2021, gold jewellery and artefacts can only be sold by BIS-registered jewellers through certified sales outlets, in compliance
with their BIS Hallmarking registration, with exceptions for exports, gold threads, items weighing less than two grams, and
consignments to BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres. The 2021 Second Amendment expanded exemptions to
include exports and re-imports under Government trade policy, domestic and international B2B exhibitions, special jewellery
types such as Kundan, Polki, and Jadaau, watches, fountain pens, and jewellers with annual turnover up to ₹40,00,000. The
2023 Amendments reinforced compliance by mandating that after March 31, 2023, no gold jewellery or artefacts may be sold,
displayed, or offered for sale without hallmarking as per IS 1417:2016 standards, while allowing sale of declared old stock
until June 30, 2023. Collectively, these Orders ensure jewellers uphold high standards of purity, traceability, and consumer
confidence, while providing a structured transition framework for existing inventory.

BIS Scheme for hallmarking of Gold and Silver Jewellery:

Hallmarking is the precise determination and official certification of the purity of precious metals in jewellery, artefacts,
bullion, or coins, serving as a critical mechanism for compliance, quality assurance, and consumer trust in the jewellery
industry. In India, the BIS hallmarking system certifies that gold and silver jewellery meet the standards set by the Bureau of
                                                                                                                           165
Indian Standards (BIS). Gold hallmarking, introduced in April 2000, follows standards such as IS 1417 (Grades of Gold and
Gold Alloys), IS 1418 (Assaying of Gold), IS 2790 (Manufacturing Guidelines for Gold Alloys), and IS 3095 (Gold Solders),
specifying primary grades of 14, 18, and 22 Carat, with amendments including 20, 23, and 24 Carat. Silver hallmarking,
effective from December 2005 under IS 2112:2014, defines six grades of silver alloys (990, 970, 925, 900, 835, 800) for
jewellery and artefacts. Compliance with these standards is mandatory for jewellery companies to ensure authenticity, build
consumer confidence, maintain traceability, and avoid legal or financial liabilities for misrepresentation. Hallmarked jewellery
also allows businesses to integrate BIS certification, register their premises, and utilize Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID)
tracking for gold, ensuring accountability across manufacturing, marketing, and sales operations.

Guidelines For Grant, Operation, Surveillance and Cancellation of Certificate of Registration of Jewellers:

The Guidelines for Grant, Operation, Surveillance, and Cancellation of Certificate of Registration (CoR) provide a
comprehensive framework for jewellery companies to legally manufacture, sell, or trade hallmarked precious metal articles.
Under these guidelines, a company must apply for a CoR from BIS, specifying the premises for hallmarking and sale, and meet
eligibility criteria including adequate infrastructure, skilled workforce, and quality control systems. Once granted, the CoR is
valid for a specified period, must be prominently displayed, and all gold and silver articles sold must conform to BIS
hallmarking standards. The guidelines mandate regular surveillance and inspections by BIS or recognized Assaying and
Hallmarking Centres to ensure compliance with purity, fineness, and operational protocols, with penalties for selling
unhallmarked or substandard items. Jewellery companies are required to maintain records of hallmarking operations, HUID
allocations for gold, and customer complaints to ensure traceability and accountability. Cancellation or suspension of the CoR
may result from repeated violations, false declarations, or failure to uphold quality standards. These guidelines ensure
transparent operations, safeguard consumer interests, maintain the integrity of the precious metals trade, and foster trust in
hallmarked jewellery.

Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism, and Combating Proliferation Financing Guidelines for
Dealers in Precious Metals and Precious Stones, 2023 (the “Guidelines) under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002,
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, and Weapons of Mass Destruction and their Delivery Systems (Prohibition of
Unlawful Activities) Act, 2005:

The Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism, and Combating Proliferation Financing Guidelines for
Dealers in Precious Metals and Precious Stones, 2023 establish a regulatory framework for jewellery companies to prevent
illicit financial activities under the PMLA, 2002, UAPA, 1967, and the Weapons of Mass Destruction (Prohibition of Unlawful
Activities) Act, 2005. Jewellery companies must implement robust Know Your Customer (KYC) and Customer Due Diligence
(CDD) procedures, particularly for high-value transactions, to verify clients’ identity, address, and financial background. They
are required to maintain comprehensive records—including invoices, receipts, and shipment documents—for traceability and
transparency, monitor for suspicious activities, and report unusual transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-
IND). Internal policies for risk assessment, employee training on AML/CFT/CPF compliance, and appointment of a designated
compliance officer are mandatory. Companies must also screen against sanctioned individuals and entities, ensure legitimate
sourcing of precious metals and stones, and prevent their operations from being used for financing terrorism, proliferation, or
other unlawful activities. Non-compliance can result in penalties, criminal liability, or suspension of business, ensuring that the
jewellery sector operates with integrity and supports national and global financial security.

The Legal Metrology Act, 2009:

The Legal Metrology Act, 2009 sets standards for weights and measures, packaging, and labeling to ensure accuracy,
transparency, and consumer protection, which are especially important for jewellery companies dealing in precious metals and
stones. Under the Act, all weighing instruments, such as digital scales and balances used for gold, silver, or gemstone
transactions, must be certified, verified, and periodically calibrated by authorized officials. Jewellery products must carry
accurate weight declarations, and pre-packaged items must display mandatory information, including net and gross weight,
metal purity, manufacturer or seller details, and maximum retail price (MRP), as per prescribed standards. Companies are also
required to maintain records of calibration, sales, and packaging for inspection by legal metrology authorities. Non-compliance,
such as misrepresentation of weight or improper labeling, can attract penalties, fines, and legal action. Adherence to the Legal
Metrology Act ensures statutory compliance, promotes fair trade, enhances consumer trust, and upholds precision and
transparency in the sale of precious metals and gemstones.




                                                                                                                         166
Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Amendment Rules, 2023 (“Packaged Commodity Rules”):

The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Amendment Rules, 2023 (“Packaged Commodity Rules”) set updated
requirements for jewellery companies regarding the packaging, labeling, and declaration of pre-packaged precious metals and
jewellery to ensure transparency and consumer protection. Under these Rules, all pre-packaged gold, silver, platinum, or
gemstone jewellery must be accurately weighed and labeled with mandatory details, including net and gross weight, metal
purity or fineness, manufacturer or packer information, maximum retail price (MRP) in Indian Rupees, and date of packing.
The Rules also require display of unique identification numbers, batch or lot numbers, and any hallmarks or certification marks
to enable traceability and authenticity verification. Jewellery companies must maintain proper records of packaging, labeling,
and calibration of weighing instruments for inspection by legal metrology authorities. Non-compliance—such as mislabeling,
inaccurate weights, or omission of mandatory information—can result in penalties, fines, or legal action. Adhering to the
Packaged Commodity Rules, 2023 helps jewellery companies ensure regulatory compliance, protect consumer rights, build
trust in product quality, and maintain accountability in the sale of precious metal jewellery and artefacts.

Payment and Settlements Systems Act, 2007:

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS Act) establishes the legal framework for regulating and supervising
payment systems in India, directly affecting jewellery companies engaged in electronic or digital transactions. Under the Act,
companies accepting payments via cards, UPI, mobile wallets, or online banking must route transactions through regulated and
authorized payment system operators (PSOs) or banks, reducing fraud risk and ensuring legal enforceability. The Act requires
timely, secure, and transparent settlement of funds between buyers and jewellers, including provisions for handling disputes,
reversals, or chargebacks. Jewellery companies offering layaway, advance payments, or EMI options must comply with norms
on settlement finality, electronic record-keeping, and transaction auditability. Compliance also aligns with Reserve Bank of
India (RBI) regulations governing digital payment infrastructure, thereby enhancing consumer confidence, financial security,
and operational transparency in high-value transactions involving gold, silver, and diamond jewellery.

Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council:

The Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC) is a statutory body established by the Government of India to
promote the export of gems and jewellery, playing a vital role for jewellery companies engaged in international trade.
Affiliation with GJEPC provides jewellery companies access to export promotion initiatives, trade fairs, and buyer-seller meets,
both domestically and globally, enhancing market reach and visibility. The Council assists companies in complying with export
regulations, quality standards, hallmarking norms, and foreign trade policies, including certification and documentation for
customs clearance and international shipments. Jewellery companies also benefit from GJEPC’s training programs, design and
technology support, and market intelligence, helping them improve product quality, adopt global trends, and remain
competitive. Additionally, GJEPC advocates for exporters’ interests with the government, addresses industry-specific
challenges, and provides guidance on tax incentives, duty drawback schemes, and trade policy benefits, supporting sustainable
growth in the global gem and jewellery industry.

All India Gems and Jewellery Domestic Council:

The All-India Gems and Jewellery Domestic Council (GJDC) is an industry body dedicated to promoting and regulating the
domestic gems and jewellery market in India, providing vital support to jewellery companies operating locally. For a jewellery
company, GJDC helps standardize trade practices, ensure ethical business conduct, and promote transparency in domestic
transactions. The Council guides compliance with regulatory requirements, including hallmarking, taxation, and consumer
protection laws, while advising on quality standards and product certification. Membership enables participation in industry
forums, exhibitions, and trade fairs, facilitating networking, marketing, and brand building. GJDC also represents domestic
jewellers’ interests with government authorities, offering advocacy on policy matters, market development initiatives, and
dispute resolution support. Additionally, it provides training, skill development, and awareness programs, enhancing
operational efficiency, compliance, and competitiveness, fostering consumer trust, and supporting the overall growth of India’s
domestic gems and jewellery sector.

Reserve Bank of India Circulars regulating Gold Loans:

RBI circulars regulating gold loans provide the framework for jewellery companies, particularly those offering gold-backed
financing or partnering with banks and NBFCs, to operate securely and compliantly. These circulars set eligibility criteria,

                                                                                                                       167
loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, interest rates, and tenure norms for loans against gold jewellery, ensuring adequate security and
adherence to RBI guidelines. They also outline documentation, reporting, and due diligence requirements, mandating proper
records of pledged gold, verification of purity and authenticity, and safeguarding of assets. Additionally, RBI directives guide
risk management practices, including insurance of pledged gold, recovery procedures in case of default, and periodic audits.
Compliance with these circulars ensures legal conformity, financial transparency, consumer protection, and mitigation of
operational and credit risks, thereby fostering trust among lenders and customers in gold loan operations.

Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002:

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, imposes statutory obligations on jewellery companies to prevent
their operations from being used for money laundering or terrorist financing. Companies must maintain detailed records of all
transactions, especially cash and high-value purchases, verify customer identities through KYC norms, and report suspicious
activities to the Financial Intelligence Unit – India (FIU-IND). Jewellery firms are required to implement internal compliance
programs, including appointing a designated reporting officer, conducting staff training, and establishing monitoring systems
to detect unusual or suspicious transactions. They must retain transaction records for the prescribed period and cooperate with
regulatory authorities during investigations. Non-compliance can result in significant penalties, including fines and attachment
of assets. Adhering to PMLA regulations ensures legal compliance, enhances credibility with banks, financial institutions, and
customers, and protects the company from reputational and financial risks associated with illicit money flows.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (the “Consumer Protection Act”) and the rules made thereunder:

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) imposes comprehensive obligations on jewellery companies to protect
consumer rights and ensure fair business practices. Companies must provide accurate information on the purity, weight, price,
and hallmarking of precious metals and stones, as well as clear policies on returns, exchanges, and warranties. They are required
to avoid unfair trade practices, including misleading advertisements or product misrepresentation, and address customer
complaints promptly and effectively. The Act empowers consumers to file complaints with Consumer Dispute Redressal
Commissions at the district, state, or national level for defective or deficient services, including issues related to jewellery
quality or delivery. Jewellery companies must maintain proper billing, documentation, and transparency to facilitate dispute
resolution and compliance with consumer rights. Non-compliance can lead to penalties, fines, and imprisonment for responsible
officers, making adherence to CPA 2019 essential for customer trust, legal compliance, and maintaining a credible market
reputation.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023:

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, provides a legal framework for jewellery companies to collect, store, process,
and transfer personal data of customers, employees, and vendors. Companies must obtain explicit consent before collecting
personal data—such as names, contact details, payment information, and transaction history—and ensure it is used only for
legitimate purposes, including order fulfillment, loyalty programs, marketing (with consent), and regulatory compliance. The
Act requires reasonable security safeguards, such as encryption, secure storage, and controlled access, to prevent unauthorized
access or breaches. Jewellery businesses must appoint a Data Protection Officer (if applicable) and maintain grievance redressal
mechanisms for addressing complaints related to data misuse. Cross-border data transfers, for instance through foreign e-
commerce platforms, must comply with consent or approved frameworks. Non-compliance can attract penalties, making
adherence essential for accountability, transparency, and consumer trust while protecting sensitive personal information in the
company’s digital operations.

TAX RELATED REGUATIONS

Income Tax Act, 1961:

The Income Tax Act, 1961, governs the computation, reporting, and payment of taxes for a jewellery company on income from
sales of jewellery, bullion, and related services. Companies must maintain accurate books of accounts covering purchases,
sales, production costs, overheads, and profits, including cash and credit transactions, to determine taxable income. The Act
requires deduction of tax at source (TDS) on salaries, contractor payments, and certain vendor payments, and tax collection at
source (TCS) on sales of precious metals and high-value goods. Profits from domestic and international sales, including exports,
are subject to corporate tax, surcharge, and applicable cess, with deductions for eligible business expenses, depreciation, and
charitable contributions. Jewellery companies must also comply with GST provisions, advance tax payments, annual income
tax filings, and, where relevant, transfer pricing rules for related-party international transactions. Non-compliance can result in


                                                                                                                         168
penalties, interest, or prosecution, making adherence essential for legal compliance and efficient financial management in the
jewellery business.

Income Tax Act, 2025 and Rules:

The Income Tax Act, 2025, effective from April 1, 2026, is the principal legislation governing the levy, computation, and
payment of income tax in India, replacing the Income Tax Act, 1961. It consolidates provisions relating to taxable income,
deductions, exemptions, TDS/TCS, assessment, appeals, and penalties, providing a simplified and modernized framework for
direct taxation. The Act is supplemented by the Income-tax Rules, 2026, which prescribe procedural and compliance
requirements, including filing of returns, maintenance of records, audit, and reporting obligations. Compliance with the Act
and Rules is mandatory for all income earned by the Company, including revenues from domestic and international jewellery
sales, ensuring proper tax administration, legal adherence, and financial transparency.

The Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (CGST Act) and Union Territory Goods and Services Tax (UTGST):

Jewellery companies operating in Union Territories without a legislature, such as Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman
& Diu, Lakshadweep, and Ladakh, are subject to the CGST Act, 2017, and the corresponding UTGST provisions. Under this
framework, intra-UT sales of goods and services, including gold, silver, diamonds, and other precious metals or stones, are
liable to CGST levied by the Central Government and UTGST levied by the respective Union Territory government. The taxes
are collected, deposited, and reported through the GST portal, with compliance obligations including proper invoicing, input
tax credit claims, and periodic return filings. Inter-UT or interstate transactions attract Integrated GST (IGST), administered
by the Central Government and apportioned between the Centre and UTs under the IGST Act. Jewellery companies must also
adhere to valuation rules, reverse charge mechanisms (where applicable), composition scheme eligibility, and maintain accurate
records of purchases and sales to ensure timely payment and avoid penalties or interest, thereby ensuring compliance with the
GST regime

Integrated Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017:

The IGST Act governs the levy and collection of Integrated Goods and Services Tax on inter-state supplies of goods and
services, including transactions by jewellery companies involving gold, silver, diamonds, gemstones, and other precious metal
or stone jewellery across state borders or from a Union Territory to a State. Under this framework, the supplier charges IGST
on invoices, collects it from the buyer, and deposits it with the Central Government, which subsequently apportions the tax
between the Centre and the destination State or Union Territory. Jewellery companies are required to maintain detailed records
of inter-state sales, proper invoicing, and utilization of input tax credits to offset IGST liability. The Act also applies to imports
and exports of jewellery, with IGST levied on imports and exports being zero-rated, allowing claims for refunds of input taxes.
Compliance with invoicing, return filing, reconciliation of IGST transactions, and timely payment is mandatory, with non-
compliance attracting interest, penalties, or legal action, ensuring that cross-border transactions of jewellery companies remain
fully GST-compliant.

Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975:

These Acts regulate the import and export of goods, including precious metals, gemstones, and jewellery, and prescribe the
applicable duties, procedures, and compliance requirements for jewellery companies. Imports of gold, silver, diamonds,
gemstones, or finished jewellery are subject to duties including Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Integrated Goods and Services
Tax (IGST), Compensation Cess, and other charges as notified by the Government. Jewellery companies importing raw
materials or finished products must comply with customs clearance procedures, such as filing bills of entry, submitting import
documentation, making valuation declarations, and adhering to BIS standards for hallmarked items. Exports of jewellery are
generally zero-rated under IGST or eligible for duty exemptions, provided documentation and compliance with the Foreign
Trade Policy are maintained. The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 prescribes specific tariff classifications and rates for different types
of precious metals, stones, and jewellery, determining the applicable duties. Non-compliance may result in penalties,
confiscation, or prosecution, making accurate record-keeping, adherence to valuation norms, and utilization of lawful
exemptions or refunds critical for jewellery companies.

ENVIRONMENT LAWS

National Environmental Policy (NEP), 2006:

NEP 2006 provides a framework for sustainable development and environmental protection in India. For a jewellery company,
it emphasizes environmentally responsible practices across all operations, including the sourcing of metals and gemstones,
                                                                                                                            169
manufacturing processes, and disposal of chemical wastes from refining, polishing, or plating activities. Companies are
expected to comply with pollution control norms, manage effluents and emissions, and adopt eco-friendly and energy-efficient
technologies to minimize environmental impact. Sustainable sourcing, including use of conflict-free or certified materials,
aligns with the policy’s focus on social and ecological responsibility. Adoption of waste reduction measures, resource-efficient
practices, and employee and customer awareness programs further integrates environmental sustainability into the business,
supporting the broader objectives of NEP 2006.

Environmental Legislations:

Jewellery companies are required to comply with environmental laws aimed at protecting natural resources, controlling
pollution, and promoting sustainability. Key regulations include the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Air (Prevention
and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Hazardous and Other
Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, and the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. Compliance
involves managing air, water, and soil pollution, safely handling chemicals used in refining or plating, treating effluents, and
ensuring proper disposal of hazardous waste. Companies are encouraged to adopt eco-friendly and energy-efficient
technologies, implement sustainable sourcing and recycling of precious metals, and reduce their carbon footprint. These
measures ensure regulatory compliance, promote corporate social responsibility, and enhance consumer trust in the brand.

Environment Impact Assessment Notification of 2006:

Jewellery companies operating facilities involving mining, metal refining, gemstone processing, or large-scale manufacturing
may fall under the EIA Notification, 2006, requiring prior environmental clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest
and Climate Change (MoEFCC) or the State Environmental Impact Assessment Authority. Compliance involves preparing an
Environmental Impact Assessment report assessing resource usage, potential air and water pollution, waste management, and
mitigation measures. Public consultation may be required for projects with significant local impact. Post-clearance, companies
must implement prescribed mitigation measures, monitor environmental parameters, and submit regular compliance reports.
Adherence to the EIA Notification ensures sustainable operations, reduces environmental liability, and aligns with corporate
social responsibility while maintaining stakeholder and consumer trust.

REGULATIONS RELATED TO FOREIGN TRADE AND INVESTMENT

The Foreign Direct Investment:

The FDI policy in India, regulated by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) and governed by
the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), provides the framework for foreign investment into Indian companies, including those in the
jewellery sector. Jewellery companies may receive FDI under the automatic route or government route, subject to sector-
specific provisions, ownership limits, and compliance with pricing and repatriation rules. FDI is permitted in manufacturing,
wholesale, and branded retail segments, with certain conditions such as local sourcing requirements, reporting of foreign equity,
dividends, and capital transactions to the RBI, and adherence to applicable caps. Compliance with the FDI policy enables access
to foreign capital, technology collaboration, global branding, and export expansion, while ensuring adherence to FEMA
regulations, corporate governance norms, and sectoral approvals.

Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (“FEMA”) and Regulations framed thereunder:

FEMA and the regulations framed thereunder govern cross-border financial transactions, foreign investments, and external
trade in India, and are critical for jewellery companies engaged in imports, exports, or foreign funding. Under FEMA, a
jewellery company must comply with RBI guidelines for receipt and remittance of foreign currency, import of gold, precious
stones, and other raw materials, repatriation of profits from foreign investments, and payments to overseas suppliers. The Act
also governs FDI, ensuring adherence to sectoral caps, automatic or government route approvals, and proper documentation of
foreign equity and profit repatriation. Jewellery companies are required to maintain records of foreign exchange transactions
for audit and reporting purposes. Non-compliance may result in penalties, confiscation of foreign exchange, or restrictions on
cross-border operations. FEMA thus provides a legal framework enabling jewellery companies to conduct international trade
and investment transparently while ensuring regulatory compliance.

Ownership restrictions of FIIs:

FIIs are permitted to invest in listed and unlisted Indian companies, including those in the jewellery sector, subject to sector-
specific caps under the FDI policy and SEBI regulations. For a jewellery company, FIIs can generally hold equity up to the

                                                                                                                        170
prescribed limits under the automatic route, while investments exceeding specified thresholds require prior approval from the
Government of India. FIIs are restricted from exercising management control or participating directly in daily operations,
ensuring that operational authority remains with Indian stakeholders. They must also comply with SEBI-mandated reporting
and disclosure requirements, including ownership declarations, transaction reporting, and adherence to pricing norms for
securities. These regulations allow jewellery companies to access foreign capital for business expansion, imports, and
technology enhancement while safeguarding strategic control and operational integrity.



Laws related to Overseas Investment by Indian Entities:

Laws governing overseas investment set out the regulatory framework under which an Indian jewellery company can invest in
foreign entities or establish operations abroad. Such investments are primarily regulated under the Foreign Exchange
Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines, including the Liberalised Remittance Scheme
(LRS) and the Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) framework. An Indian jewellery company may invest in foreign subsidiaries,
joint ventures, or acquire stakes in overseas businesses, subject to prescribed limits, reporting obligations, and approval
routes—automatic or government route—depending on the sector and transaction value. Compliance requires filing of
prescribed forms with the RBI, maintaining proper accounting records, and ensuring that the overseas investment aligns with
the company’s core activities, such as retail, manufacturing, sourcing of precious metals, or branding. Repatriation of profits,
dividends, or sale proceeds must adhere to regulatory guidelines, while anti-money laundering, taxation, and transfer pricing
norms are also applicable, ensuring legal, financial, and operational transparency in the jewellery company’s cross-border
investments.

Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 (“FTDRA 1992”):

The FTDRA 1992 provides the statutory framework governing import and export activities in India, including for jewellery
companies, with the objective of promoting foreign trade, regulating trade practices, and ensuring compliance with international
agreements. For a jewellery company, the Act enables lawful export of gold, silver, precious stones, and finished jewellery, as
well as import of raw materials such as gold, silver, diamonds, gemstones, and specialized machinery. Under the Act,
companies must obtain an Importer Exporter Code (IEC) from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) to conduct
cross-border trade. Jewellery companies are also required to comply with applicable export promotion schemes, such as the
Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) or its successor, the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products
(RoDTEP), to avail incentives. Compliance with customs procedures, licensing requirements for restricted or prohibited goods,
hallmarking and quality certification standards, and anti-money laundering obligations is mandatory. Non-compliance,
including misdeclarations or contravention of trade norms, can attract penalties, fines, or legal action, making adherence to the
FTDRA 1992 essential for smooth, lawful international operations.

Foreign Trade Policy 2023:

The Foreign Trade Policy 2023 provides the regulatory framework and incentives for promoting India’s exports and regulating
imports, with direct implications for jewellery companies engaged in cross-border trade. For a jewellery company, the policy
outlines schemes such as the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products (RoDTEP), Export Promotion Capital Goods
(EPCG), and Duty Drawback, which help reduce costs on exported gold, silver, diamonds, gemstones, and finished jewellery
products. It mandates compliance with quality standards, BIS hallmarking for gold and silver jewellery, and adherence to
customs documentation and licensing requirements for importing raw materials, machinery, or precious stones. The policy also
encourages value addition under the “Make in India” initiative, promoting domestic manufacturing and processing before
export. Additionally, it provides guidance on procedures for claiming export incentives, simplified registration through the
Importer Exporter Code (IEC), and enforcement mechanisms to prevent trade fraud, smuggling, or violations of
restricted/prohibited goods lists. Compliance ensures jewellery companies are eligible for export benefits, maintain smooth
international operations, and contribute to India’s broader trade and economic objectives.

LAWS RELATED TO EMPLOYMENT OF MANPOWER

The Code on Wages, 2019:

For jewellery companies, the Code on Wages, 2019—effective from November 21, 2025—has significant implications due to
the sector’s reliance on a diverse workforce, including skilled artisans (goldsmiths, polishers, setters), shop-floor sales staff,
contract labour, and home-based or unorganized workers. Companies must ensure that all categories of employees, whether
engaged in manufacturing units, boutiques, or ancillary workshops, are remunerated in accordance with the revised statutory
                                                                                                                         171
definition of “wages,” applicable minimum wages (including notified floor wages), and gender-neutral pay norms, with timely
disbursal and correct bonus calculations. Payroll structures should be updated, contractor arrangements reviewed, and historical
practices such as piece-rate or cash payments regularized to prevent contraventions. Jewellery companies are required to assess
the impact of wage restructuring on margins, inventory costing, and profitability, while disclosing any pending wage, bonus,
or equal-remuneration disputes—common in labour-intensive jewellery clusters—as material risks. These must be reflected in
restated financial statements and addressed in the Management Discussion & Analysis, ensuring full compliance under the
Code.


Industrial Relations Code, 2020:

For jewellery companies, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020—effective from November 21, 2025—is particularly relevant
due to the sector’s labour-intensive operations, clustered manufacturing units, and reliance on skilled artisans, boutiques staff,
and contract or fixed-term workers. Companies must comply with provisions relating to standing orders (applicable to
establishments with 300 or more workers), maintain properly documented service conditions, and ensure fixed-term
employment contracts are aligned with the Code for seasonal or project-based demands. Special attention is required for past
or ongoing labour unrest, union activity in manufacturing hubs, retrenchment, or workshop closures, ensuring adherence to
procedural safeguards, compensation norms, and contributions to the Re-skilling Fund where applicable. Jewellery companies
are expected to identify and quantify any financial exposure arising from industrial disputes, retrenchment liabilities, or
workforce reclassification, and reflect these in financial statements and disclosures, ensuring that operations, cost structures,
and continuity of skilled labour are not materially affected by non-compliance under the Industrial Relations Code.

Code on Social Security, 2020:

For jewellery companies, the Code on Social Security, 2020 is particularly significant given the sector’s extensive use of
contract labour, fixed-term artisans, boutiques staff, and, in certain cases, home-based or unorganized workers engaged in
polishing, finishing, or allied activities. Companies must ensure that all eligible employees are properly identified and provided
with mandatory social security coverage under the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), Employees’ State
Insurance Corporation (ESIC), gratuity, maternity benefits, and employee compensation in accordance with the Code, including
expanded gratuity eligibility for fixed-term employees. Proper digitized registration, record-keeping, and timely contribution
remittance are essential. Jewellery companies are expected to quantify any historical gaps in provident fund or ESIC
contributions, under-provisioning of gratuity liabilities, or non-compliance in contractor-managed labour, and reflect these in
restated financial statements. Potential exposure to penalties, interest, or employee claims must be recognized as material risks
and disclosed in outstanding litigation records, ensuring that compliance with the Code on Social Security does not give rise to
material legal, financial, or operational risk for the business.

Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020:

For jewellery companies, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020—effective from November 21,
2025—is particularly relevant due to the sector’s reliance on factory-based manufacturing units, small workshops, and contract
or migrant labour for processes such as casting, polishing, electroplating, and stone setting, which involve exposure to
chemicals, heat, and precision machinery. Companies must ensure compliance with prescribed safety standards, including
adequate ventilation, fire-safety systems, periodic health check-ups, welfare facilities, regulated working hours, and statutory
leave provisions. Proper registration, licensing, and record-keeping for factories, contract labour, and inter-state migrant
workers are mandatory. Any gaps in safety infrastructure, workplace accidents, non-compliance notices, or pending
proceedings under the Code can give rise to operational disruptions, financial liabilities, and reputational risk, and therefore
require proactive identification, remediation, and disclosure in statutory and financial records to ensure lawful and sustainable
operations.

Employees’ Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976:

For a jewellery company, the EDLI Scheme, 1976, provides life insurance coverage to all employees registered under the
Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) scheme. All employees working in manufacturing units (goldsmiths, polishers), retail outlets
(salespersons, cashiers), or corporate offices who are EPF members are automatically covered under the scheme. In the event
of an employee’s death during service, the nominee receives a lump sum insurance amount linked to the employee’s average
monthly wages and EPF balance, subject to the maximum insured limit as periodically revised by the government. The
employer contributes a small percentage of the employee’s monthly wages (as part of the overall EPF contribution) to the EDLI
fund, with no separate employee contribution required. Employees are required to designate nominees, and the jewellery
company facilitates claims settlement through the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), ensuring prompt payment
to the nominee. The company must maintain accurate records of employees, wages, and EPF contributions, and submit periodic
                                                                                                                         172
returns to the EPFO. Additional benefits, such as accidental death-cum-disability coverage, may also be provided, ensuring
that all personnel, whether engaged in high-risk manufacturing processes or low-risk retail operations, have guaranteed life
insurance protection linked to their employment.

Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020:

The OSHWC Code, 2020, establishes a comprehensive framework for the safety, health, and welfare of employees across all
operations of a jewellery company. It applies to employees in manufacturing units (goldsmiths, polishers, casting and finishing
staff), retail stores (sales personnel, cashiers), warehouses, and administrative offices. Key requirements include provision of
personal protective equipment (PPE), safe working machinery, adequate ventilation, fire safety protocols, periodic health
check-ups, and medical facilities for employees exposed to occupational hazards. The Code also mandates regulated working
hours, weekly offs, overtime rules, welfare amenities such as rest areas, canteens, creche facilities, proper lighting and
ergonomics, as well as training in safe handling of tools, chemicals, and emergency procedures. Jewellery companies must
maintain records of employees, incidents, occupational diseases, and compliance reports, which are subject to inspection by
authorities, with non-compliance attracting fines or legal action. Compliance ensures a safe and healthy work environment for
all employees while fulfilling statutory obligations under the Code

Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986:

The Act prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any jewellery company operations, including manufacturing,
retail, or administrative functions. Adolescents aged 14–18 years may only be employed in non-hazardous roles, such as clerical
work or packaging, and are strictly barred from hazardous processes like metal melting, chemical polishing, or operating heavy
machinery. The Act mandates limits on working hours, rest periods, and prohibition of night work for adolescents. Jewellery
companies are required to maintain registers of adolescent workers, verify age proof, ensure safe working conditions, and
comply with government inspections. Non-compliance can attract fines, imprisonment, or both. Additionally, companies are
encouraged to prevent indirect or contract-based child labour in their supply chain, thereby promoting ethical labour practices
and safeguarding legal compliance.

Fire Prevention Laws and The National Building Code of India, 2016:

These laws provide the regulatory framework for fire safety and structural compliance across jewellery company facilities,
including manufacturing units, workshops, warehouses, and retail boutiques. Companies must implement fire detection and
alarm systems, smoke detectors, sprinklers, fire extinguishers, and clearly marked emergency exits, particularly in areas
handling flammable materials such as polishing chemicals or metal dust. Compliance with NBC guidelines on safe occupancy,
fire-resistant construction, proper ventilation, and electrical safety is mandatory. Jewellery companies are required to obtain
No Objection Certificates (NOCs) from local fire authorities, conduct regular fire drills, train staff on emergency procedures,
appoint fire safety officers, and maintain logs of fire safety equipment. Additional precautions include safe storage of
combustible materials, separation of chemical and heat-intensive processes, and adherence to prescribed safety distances. Non-
compliance can result in fines, closure, or legal liability. Integration with the OSHWC Code ensures a comprehensive approach
to occupational safety, protecting employees, visitors, and high-value inventory from fire hazards.

The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressed) Act, 2013:

This Act establishes a legal framework to prevent, prohibit, and redress sexual harassment of women across all jewellery
company operations, including manufacturing units, workshops, retail boutiques, warehouses, and administrative offices. It
covers all women employees—permanent, temporary, contractual, or trainees. Jewellery companies are required to create a
safe workplace, implement anti-harassment policies, display ICC notices, conduct awareness programs, and constitute an
Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) at each establishment with ten or more employees. The ICC handles complaints
confidentially, investigates incidents, and recommends remedial action. Employers must ensure non-retaliation, assist
complainants, maintain records, and submit annual reports to the District Officer. Non-compliance can result in fines or
disciplinary action. Regular training and sensitization programs are mandated to promote a respectful, inclusive, and
harassment-free work environment.

Chandigarh Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1958:

This Act governs employment terms, working conditions, and employee rights in retail and service establishments, including
jewellery boutiques, offices, warehouses, and workshops in Chandigarh. It covers all categories of employees—permanent,
temporary, and contractual. Jewellery companies must comply with prescribed working hours, weekly offs, overtime pay, leave

                                                                                                                       173
entitlements, and public holidays. The Act requires maintenance of employee registers, employment contracts, and age
verification for apprentices or trainees. It also mandates safe working conditions, provision of drinking water, sanitation, and
welfare facilities, particularly in workshops handling polishing, casting, or chemicals. Timely payment of wages, allowances,
and overtime is required, and authorities may inspect establishments to enforce compliance. Non-compliance can attract fines
or legal action. Overall, the Act ensures that jewellery companies in Chandigarh operate with regulated work practices,
safeguarding employee rights and maintaining a safe and structured work environment.




LAWS RELATING TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY

Intellectual property in India is safeguarded under both common law and statutory frameworks. Statutory protection includes
patents under the Patents Act, 1970, copyrights under the Copyright Act, 1957, and trademarks under the Trade Marks Act,
1999, which provide civil and criminal remedies against infringement. India is also a signatory to key international IP treaties,
including the Patent Cooperation Treaty, 1970, the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, 1883, the Berne
Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, 1886, the Universal Copyright Convention, 1952, and the
International Convention for the Protection of Performers, Producers of Phonograms and Broadcasting Organizations, 1961.
As a member of the World Trade Organization, India adheres to the TRIPS Agreement, ensuring compliance with global IP
standards. This framework enables jewellery companies to protect designs, trademarks, branding, and other intellectual assets,
while providing legal recourse against infringement.

Trade Marks Act, 1999 (“Trade Marks Act”):

The Trade Marks Act, 1999 provides the legal framework for protecting brand identity, logos, designs, and other distinctive
marks of a jewellery company. This includes registration and protection of trademarks for brand names, hallmarks, logos, and
product-specific marks used in boutiques, packaging, or marketing. Jewellery companies must ensure trademarks are
distinctive, not deceptively similar to existing marks, and capable of differentiating their products in the market. The Act grants
exclusive rights to use, license, or prevent unauthorized use of registered marks, including against counterfeiting or imitation
in retail, e-commerce, or promotional activities. Legal remedies include injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing goods.
Trademarks are valid for ten years and can be renewed indefinitely, with companies required to maintain records and monitor
expiry. Well-known trademarks enjoy protection even without formal registration. Compliance with procedural requirements,
including filing applications and responding to objections with the Trademark Registry, enables jewellery companies to
safeguard brand reputation, secure market presence, and prevent misuse of their intellectual property in domestic and
international markets.

Copyright Act, 1957 and the rules made thereunder:

The Copyright Act, 1957, and the rules made thereunder, provide legal protection for original works of authorship, including
jewellery designs, CAD models, sketches, artistic creations, marketing content, promotional materials, and software used by
the company. Copyright arises automatically upon creation, though registration with the Copyright Office enhances
enforceability. The Act grants the company or designer exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, display, sell, or license these
works and prevents unauthorized copying or commercial exploitation. Remedies for infringement include injunctions, damages,
and seizure of infringing materials. Moral rights enable designers to claim attribution and prevent distortion of their works,
which is particularly relevant for signature jewellery collections. Copyright for artistic works lasts for the life of the author plus
60 years, while corporate works such as software or advertisements have defined terms. The company must also ensure
compliance with third-party copyrights when using external content and can license its own works for collaborations,
marketing, or e-commerce. This framework allows the jewellery company to safeguard creativity, original designs, and digital
assets while protecting its intellectual property rights in domestic and international markets.

Design Act, 2000:

The Designs Act, 2000, provides legal protection for the aesthetic and ornamental aspects of jewellery, safeguarding original
patterns, motifs, gemstone arrangements, carvings, and decorative elements from unauthorized copying or imitation. Protection
under the Act requires that designs be new or original, applied to an article, and pertain to visual appearance rather than
functional features. Registration with the Designs Registry grants the company exclusive rights to manufacture, sell, or license
the design and prevents others from reproducing or commercially exploiting it without permission. The protection term is 10

                                                                                                                            174
years from the date of registration, extendable by 5 years. Applications must include representations or photographs of the
design and payment of prescribed fees. Remedies for infringement include injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing
jewellery. This framework enables the jewellery company to secure its ornamental innovations, uphold brand prestige, deter
counterfeiting, and maintain competitive advantage in domestic and international markets.

Patents Act, 1970:

The Patents Act, 1970, provides legal protection for inventions and innovative processes in jewellery manufacturing, design,
and technology, ensuring exclusivity and commercial advantage. Patentable subject matter includes novel methods of metal
processing, gemstone setting, alloy formulation, CAD/CAM-based manufacturing techniques, and unique tools or machinery
used in production. To be patentable, inventions must be new, involve an inventive step, and be industrially applicable. Filing
with the Patent Office requires disclosure of technical details, examination, and payment of prescribed fees. Registered patents
confer exclusive rights to manufacture, use, sell, or license the invention for 20 years from the filing date, while infringement
remedies include injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing products. Provisions for compulsory licensing ensure public
interest, and maintenance obligations, including timely fee payments and record-keeping, are required to retain patent rights.
This framework enables the jewellery company to protect technological innovations, foster creativity, safeguard investment,
and maintain a competitive edge in domestic and international markets.

OTHER GENERAL RULES AND REGULATIONS

The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (“MSME Act”):

The MSME Development Act, 2006 provides a framework to promote, develop, and protect micro, small, and medium
enterprises engaged in jewellery manufacturing, wholesale, and allied services. Jewellery units are classified based on
investment in plant, machinery, or equipment, and eligible units can obtain Udyam registration to access statutory benefits,
credit facilities, and government schemes. The Act facilitates priority lending, subsidized loans, and working capital support,
ensuring timely payments from buyers with recourse to the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council in case of delays.
It also promotes technological adoption, including CAD/CAM systems, and skill development for artisans, while providing
access to government exhibitions, marketing assistance, and export incentives. Compliance with registration, record-keeping,
and reporting obligations is required to retain benefits. This framework ensures MSME jewellery companies receive financial,
technological, and legal support, fostering growth, innovation, and sustainability in the sector.

General Criminal Laws:

Jewellery companies and their directors, officers, and employees are subject to India’s general criminal laws, including the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
These statutes govern substantive criminal offences, procedural safeguards, and the admissibility and evaluation of evidence,
and are particularly relevant in contexts such as gold or gemstone fraud, misrepresentation, employee misconduct, money
laundering, regulatory non-compliance, or workplace incidents. Non-compliance may expose the company and its personnel
to civil or criminal liability, penalties, or regulatory action, potentially impacting business operations, financial condition, and
reputation. Accordingly, implementation of robust internal controls, employee training, and legal compliance mechanisms is
critical to mitigate such risks.

State Laws:

Jewellery companies operating in Chandigarh are subject to state-specific regulations, primarily under the Chandigarh Shops
and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1958, as well as local fire safety, labour
welfare, and municipal compliance requirements. All boutiques, manufacturing units, workshops, warehouses, and
administrative offices must register under the Act, maintain statutory employee records including proof of age for apprentices
or trainees, and ensure compliance with prescribed working hours, overtime, leave, public holidays, and timely payment of
wages for goldsmiths, polishers, sales staff, and clerical employees. Companies must adhere to local health, sanitation, and
occupational safety standards, provide drinking water, restrooms, and safe working conditions for chemical polishing, metal
casting, and other manufacturing processes, and comply with fire safety and building regulations under the National Building
Code of India (NBC), 2016, including installation of fire extinguishers, emergency exits, and obtaining necessary fire NOCs.
Compliance with taxation and licensing requirements, including GST, professional tax, municipal trade licenses, and weights
and measures standards, is mandatory. Local authorities may conduct inspections, and any violation of employment, safety, or
municipal regulations can attract fines, closure orders, or legal action, ensuring that jewellery companies in Chandigarh operate
within lawful, safe, and regulated frameworks.

                                                                                                                          175
Municipality Laws:

For a jewellery company operating in Chandigarh, compliance with municipality laws primarily involves regulations issued by
the Chandigarh Municipal Corporation (CMC) governing trade licensing, building use, taxation, public safety, and
environmental standards. All boutiques, workshops, and storage facilities must obtain valid trade licenses with timely renewals,
while premises must adhere to the National Building Code (NBC) and local zoning rules to ensure structural safety, fire exits,
emergency routes, and commercial occupancy compliance. Companies are required to maintain health, sanitation, and proper
disposal of chemical or metallic waste from polishing and casting operations, along with adequate employee and customer
facilities. Fire safety measures, including installation of extinguishers, smoke detectors, and emergency evacuation protocols,
must meet municipal norms, with periodic inspections by authorities. Signage and advertisements must comply with CMC
regulations regarding size, location, and illumination, while property taxes, water charges, and other local levies must be timely
paid. The CMC retains inspection and enforcement powers, and non-compliance may attract fines, closure orders, or legal
action, ensuring that jewellery operations in Chandigarh remain lawful, safe, and socially responsible.

MAIN OBJECTS OF OUR COMPANY

The main object(s) of our Company, as contained in our Memorandum of Association, are as set forth below:

    1.    To carry on all or any of the business of goldsmiths, silver smiths, jewellers, gem and diamond merchants and of
          manufacturing and dealing in clocks, watches, jewellery, cutlery and their components and accessories and of
          producing acquiring and trading in metals, bullion, gold ornaments, silver utensils, diamond, precious stones, paintings,
          manuscripts, antiques and objects of art.

                                                                                                                         178
    2.    To carry on the trades of business of gold smiths, silver smiths, enamellers, jewellers, gem merchants, electroplates,
         importers and exporters of bullion and other refined and smelted metals.
    3.   To carry on business as goldsmiths, silversmiths Jewellers, gem merchants, importers and exporters of bullion and
         buy, sell and deal (wholesale and retail) in bullion precious stones, jewellery gold or silver cups, shields, articles of
         virtue objects of art.
    4.   To carry on business as goldsmiths, silversmiths, jewellers, gem merchants and importers and exporters of bullion and
         to buy, sell and deal in (wholesale or retail) precious stones, jewellery, gold and silver plate, electroplate, bronzes,
         articles or various objects of art and to manufacture and to establish factories for manufacturing goods for the above
         business.
    5.    To carry on in India or elsewhere the business to manufacture, produce, process, prepare, commercialise, cut, polish,
         set, design, display, exchange, examine, finish, grind, grade, assort, import, export, buy, sell, resale, demonstrate,
         market and to act as agent, broker, indentor, liasioner, adatias, representative, C & F agents, export house, valuer,
         sales promoter, supplier, provider, merchants, stockists, distributor, wholesaler, retailer or otherwise to deal in all
         shapes, sizes, varieties, description, specifications, applications & designs of rough, raw, cut, uncut, polished or
         processed, natural & man made precious semiprecious & natural stones such as diamonds, ruby, pearls, gemstones,
         blue sapphires, cat's eye stone, coral, topaz, opal, zircon, tourmaline, jade, spinel ruby, aquamarine, turquoise, peidot,
         agate, garnet, corundum, amethyst, malachite, citrine, alexendrite, smoky quartz, lapis lazuli, rock crystal, onyx, moon
         stone, jasper, blood stone, gold stone, bismuth, jet, diopside, tiger eye, sunstone, spinal, jews stone, load stoner,
         sardonex, touch stone, amber and their ornaments, jewelleries, articles, goods, or things, made in the combination of
         gold, silver, platinum, or other metals, and alloys thereof and for the purpose to act as goldsmith, silversmith, jewelers,
         gem merchants, electroplaters, polishers, purifiers, and to do all incidental acts and things necessary for the attainment
         of above objects.
